Contribution: C1 Cost model for peer selection
Exact claim: Under a MAC count of the two attention products, a score-then-select rule removes at most half of the forward-pass attention arithmetic: C_dense/C_topk = 2N/(N+k) < 2.
Theoretical support: Prop. 1 (Sec. 3.2), proof App. A.1; diagonal convention and A1-A6 in App. A.1
Experimental support: FLOP counter on composed paths (Sec. 4.2 Q1; App. B 'What each implementation executes'): gathered executes the reduction, masked does not
Scope: Forward pass; equal key/value widths; projections and selection cost excluded
Limitation: Ceiling is 1 + d_v/d_k for unequal widths (can exceed 2 if d_v > d_k); training analogue 6N/(N+5k) is a separate statement
Required wording: 'removes at most half of the forward-pass attention arithmetic (equal key and value widths)'; never 'at most half of the cost' or 'of the time'

Exact claim: Charging the selector's own cost C_sel gives S = 2N^2 d / (2Nkd + C_sel); with k,d fixed and N->inf: full-score <2, all-pairs in p dims -> 2d/(gamma p), Theta(N log N) selector -> Theta(N/log N), linear cNkd -> 2N/((2+c)k), free -> N/k.
Theoretical support: Prop. 2, Cor. 1 (Sec. 3.3), proofs App. A.3; closed forms App. A.4
Experimental support: Pre-score sweeps (Sec. 4.6, Tab. selectors, Fig. prescore): all-pairs selector cost grows ~quadratically, grid ~linearly, Z-order nearly flat
Scope: Asymptotic, MAC-equivalent unit convention; finite N <= 512
Limitation: Asymptotic classes do not predict finite-N ordering on their own: grid (case d) is slower than all-pairs (case b) at k=16 for N in {384,512}; measured selector cost is traffic, not arithmetic
Required wording: 'sorts selectors into four asymptotic classes'; state that the finite-N ranking is set by constants the count does not see

Exact claim: Gathering the k retained value rows is traffic-neutral relative to reading the N-wide weight row only when kd <= N.
Theoretical support: Sec. 3.4, simplified accounting (each tensor read/written once; cache ignored)
Experimental support: Sec. 4.3: at d=16,N=512,k=128 the composed gather moves ~4x the bytes and is 37x slower; head-width sweep reverses at d>=64 (App. B.3)
Scope: Per-query compaction of the aggregation operand; fp32
Limitation: Not a GPU performance model; ignores cache, writes vs reads asymmetry, index bytes and the score write; used as a pre-implementation screen
Required wording: 'a pre-implementation traffic criterion under the stated accounting'

Exact claim: Masked, gathered (composed) and fused implementations of one function, verified equivalent, against a dense baseline that is the best of the vendor library, a dense Triton kernel searched over the same space and filter, and (Sec. 4.5) FlexAttention; three numerical formats.
Experimental support: Tab. headline, autotune, precision; App. B verification (158 configs); new fixed-set sweep (results/fixed_set.json)
Scope: One GPU architecture (sm_120), shared device, unlocked clocks; N <= 512; d 16-512
Limitation: Sparse search admits 3 configs above N=192 vs 28-106 dense; no streaming exact top-k
Required wording: 'best implementation found under our search and admissibility constraints'; never 'optimal'

Contribution: C3 When sparse attention is faster (score-then-select)
Exact claim: Composed score-then-select is slower than the best dense at every configuration measured; fused score-then-select is faster only at k=1 (and k=2 at one configuration), d in {16,32}, fp32 without tensor cores; with TF32/bf16 dense the advantage is gone from N=384.
Theoretical support: Prop. 1 bounds the arithmetic saving; byte criterion explains composed loss
Experimental support: Tab. headline, crossover, precision; Fig. ksweep; fixed-set sweep shows finding the set is most of the fused kernel's cost
Scope: N in [192,512], d=16/32 for the crossover; fp32/TF32/bf16
Limitation: k=1 is a degenerate attention (one-element softmax); crossover is conditional on a dense kernel that does not use tensor cores
Required wording: 'faster only when one peer is retained ... and only without tensor cores'; flag k=1 degeneracy wherever the crossover is cited

Exact claim: Given the retained set, fused attention over it is up to 16x faster than dense (N=512, k=2); end to end the selector decides: all-pairs and grid selectors lose, the Z-order selector reaches parity (0.86x on minima) at N=512, k=4, the largest N measured.
Experimental support: Tab. selectors, prescore; second sweep replication; median reversal in one sweep
Scope: d=16, batch 256, fp32, N <= 512; selectors attend to different peers than top-k
Limitation: End-to-end parity is a best-case (minimum) result that the paired median reverses in one of two sweeps; selector quality not compared
Required wording: Separate 'attention stage' (16x) from 'end-to-end' (parity at N=512 on minima); never attach the 16x to a selector
